headline_fact: Mint, lime and a little fizz: a drink shaped by the way it is mixed.
summary: A Mojito combines rum, lime, sugar, mint and soda over ice. Its identity comes from their balance, rather than one ingredient alone.
did_you_know: The mint is part of the aromatic base, while the soda lengthens the drink. The finished glass combines citrus, sweetness and a fresh herbal aroma.
core_mechanics: Soda contains dissolved carbon dioxide. Opening the container lowers the pressure above it, allowing gas to leave the liquid. Temperature also affects how much remains dissolved.
why_it_matters: Understand its ingredients, separate origin stories from evidence, and make a practical alcohol-free interpretation.

in_depth_breakdown.real_world_application: A trolley carrying more mass needs more net force to achieve the same acceleration.

learning_takeaways: Mixing order changes the finished glass.
Keep origin stories separate from established evidence.

identity.name: Mojito
identity.strength_context: The classic includes rum. Strength varies with the rum, proportions and dilution; the recipe below is an alcohol-free interpretation.

drinks_lesson.hook: Mint, lime and a little fizz: a drink shaped by the way it is mixed.
drinks_lesson.question: What makes a Mojito more than lime-flavoured soda?
drinks_lesson.learning_goal: Understand its ingredients, separate origin stories from evidence, and make a practical alcohol-free interpretation.

introduction.explanation: A Mojito combines rum, lime, sugar, mint and soda over ice. Its identity comes from their balance, rather than one ingredient alone.
introduction.what_makes_it_unique: The mint is part of the aromatic base, while the soda lengthens the drink. The finished glass combines citrus, sweetness and a fresh herbal aroma.
introduction.cultural_role: The drink belongs to Cuban cocktail culture. Its international popularity also produces adaptations that deserve their own names and context.

origin.account: The Mojito is associated with Cuba. Accounts of its predecessors connect lime, sugar, mint and a cane spirit.
origin.evidence_and_uncertainty: The exact invention story is disputed. A story about a precursor is not proof of one inventor or a single creation date.

history.why_it_changed: Historical accounts describe earlier combinations, but the connection to the modern recipe needs careful qualification.
The IBA recipe specifies the ingredients and order. It provides a contemporary reference point without settling every historical claim.

then_and_now.earlier_method: Accounts of predecessors describe mint, lime, sugar and a cane spirit. The evidence does not establish one universal early recipe.
then_and_now.modern_method: The IBA method mixes mint, sugar and lime, adds soda and ice, then rum and more soda with a light stir.
then_and_now.what_changed: The documented contemporary recipe gives bartenders a shared reference. Local ingredients and personal methods still vary.
then_and_now.what_remains: The combination of citrus, sweetness, mint and a cane-spirit base remains central to the classic.

sensory_profile.flavour: Sweet and citrus-led, with the rum present in the classic.
sensory_profile.finish: Citrus and mint remain after the sip.

ingredients.name: Mint
ingredients.role: An aromatic ingredient in the mixed base.
ingredients.effect: Different mint varieties can change the aroma.

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.role: Provides the citrus part of the balance.
ingredients.effect: Fresh juice brings acidity alongside the sugar.

ingredients.name: Soda water
ingredients.effect: It makes the drink longer and sparkling.

production_steps.title: Build the base
production_steps.explanation: Mix mint with sugar and lime juice. These ingredients form the starting balance.
production_steps.what_to_notice: The mint is mixed into the drink, rather than serving only as decoration.

production_steps.title: Finish over ice
production_steps.explanation: The IBA method adds soda and ice, then rum and more soda. A light stir brings the ingredients together.
production_steps.what_to_notice: The final mixing is light, rather than a vigorous shake of the carbonated drink.

science.title: Why the soda releases bubbles
science.mechanism: Carbon dioxide leaves the liquid when conditions change.
science.explanation: Soda contains dissolved carbon dioxide. Opening the container lowers the pressure above it, allowing gas to leave the liquid. Temperature also affects how much remains dissolved.
science.observable_cue: Freshly opened soda bubbles; a glass left standing gradually loses fizz.
science.limits: The exact bubble rate also depends on the liquid, container and other conditions. This explanation does not calculate an exact carbonation level.

recipe.title: A lime-and-pudina cooler
recipe.traditional_preparation: The IBA Mojito includes white rum. This home version leaves it out and sets explicit soda and ice amounts for a repeatable example.
recipe.adaptation_notes: Use fresh pudina and locally available lime. This is an alcohol-free interpretation, rather than an exact copy of the Cuban cocktail.

ingredients.name: Chilled soda water
ingredients.role: Lengthens the drink and adds fizz

substitutions.quantity: Use the listed six sprigs, then adjust aroma to taste.
substitutions.effect: Mint varieties differ, so the aroma can change.

steps.title: Mix the aromatic base
steps.instruction: Mix the lime juice, sugar and mint in the glass.
steps.doneness_cue: The ingredients form an even base.

steps.title: Add ice and chilled soda
steps.instruction: Add the ice, then pour in the soda water. Stir lightly to combine.
steps.doneness_cue: The glass is cold and the soda still bubbles.

variations.name: An alcohol-free interpretation
variations.difference: The rum is omitted, so the result has a different flavour balance.
variations.how_it_developed: It adapts the mint, lime and soda combination for a different preference. No single birthplace is claimed here.
variations.evidence_and_uncertainty: This is the adaptation used in the local recipe, not a claim about a documented invention.

variations.name: A local-mint adaptation
variations.difference: Locally available pudina replaces a specified Cuban mint.
variations.how_it_developed: Ingredient access shapes the preparation. The substitution changes aroma, so it is stated explicitly.
variations.evidence_and_uncertainty: This is an illustrative kitchen adaptation, not a named historical regional cocktail.

serving_context.glassware: A tall glass provides room for the ice and soda.
serving_context.pairing_and_customs: The IBA garnish uses mint and a lime slice. Serving choices can vary with the setting.
serving_context.alcohol_free_option: Follow the measured pudina-and-lime recipe on this page for an alcohol-free interpretation.
serving_context.practical_notes: Use fresh ingredients and chilled soda. If making the classic, use a commercially produced rum that is legally available to you.

troubleshooting.cause: The dissolved gas leaves the liquid after opening.
troubleshooting.fix: Add chilled soda near serving time and mix lightly.

knowledge_checks.question: Does removing rum leave the classic unchanged?
knowledge_checks.answer: No. It creates an alcohol-free interpretation.
knowledge_checks.explanation: The spirit contributes flavour as well as alcohol. A useful adaptation makes that change clear.

takeaways: Mixing order changes the finished glass.
Keep origin stories separate from established evidence.
